newsitem.title: HAITI: Haitian popular organizations call general strike.
newsitem.headline: Haitian popular organizations call general strike.

text.p: Militant opponents of Haiti's government on Wednesday threatened violence against anyone failing to honor a general strike demanding the prime minister's resignation and sweeping economic policy changes.

"The streets had better be empty Thursday or they will run with red, red, red," said a representative of one of hundreds of popular organizations said to be sponsoring the strike. He declined to give his name during a radio appearance.

An umbrella group calling itself "Koupe Tet, Boule Kay," the Creole words for "Cutting Heads and Burning Houses" after the rallying cry of Haiti's bloody 1803 slave revolt, sent facsimile messages to businesses in Port-au-Prince warning they should be closed or risk violent retribution.

The Haitian Press Agency reported that the strike was under way by mid-afternoon on Wednesday in the northern city of Cap-Haitien and that at least three people were wounded in a clash between police and demonstrators who set up barricades of burning tires and threw bottles and rocks.

The strike was the latest in a series of violent events in Port-au-Prince. Gangs have terrorized the city in recent weeks, leaving at least 19 people dead including three police officers, according to the United Nations.
In the past week alone, the Justice Ministry's Security chief was killed at a busy intersection in broad daylight and a senator survived a gunshot to his head.

Haitian National Police Chief Pierre Denize and Security Secretary Robert Manuel met with parliamentarians on Wednesday to discuss security strategies. Manuel called it bizarre that the groups would threaten more violence in the midst of a crime wave.
"If someone decides to go to work or a journalist is killed, as far as I'm concerned these popular organizations are responsible for murder," he told reporters.

Haitian grassroots organizations have been calling for Prime Minister Rosny Smarth to step down, criticizing government plans to privatize nine state-run enterprises such as the telephone and electricity companies.
Smarth disseminated a statement on Wednesday denouncing the strike. "The government will respond strongly to any attack meant to destabilize or disturb the public order," it said.

The general strike would be the second in two months, following a work stoppage called by popular organizations on Jan. 16. Burning tire barricades and rock-throwing protesters were intimidating enough that most people stayed home.

President Rene Preval acknowledged the dissatisfaction of those who called the strike, but said he did not plan to give in to the organizations' demands. "A relatively small group of people cannot bring the country to a halt unless the population agrees with them," he said after that protest.
Smarth, who recently marked his first anniversary as prime minister, said he would not resign unless asked to by Preval.

"If we are going to make changes, we shouldn't just do so for the sake of making changes," Smarth told Reuters in a recent interview. "We need to study what is wrong and what needs to be done for the greater good."
Strike organizers also planned a demonstration in front of U.N. offices on Thursday to demand that its troops leave because "they do nothing to provide a climate of security."

Foreign troops have been in Haiti since September 1994, when a force of 20,000 led by the United States landed to oust leaders of a military coup and restore Jean-Bertrand Aristide, Haiti's first freely elected president.

Preval, an Aristide protege, succeeded Aristide as Haiti's president last February, but has not enjoyed the popular support of his predecessor, who was constitutionally barred from serving consecutive terms as president but remains Haiti's most popular political figure.

The 1,500 U.N. troops now in Haiti are scheduled to leave on July 31. Preval has said he would not ask for a further extension of the peacekeeping mission, leading to widespread fears about long-term instability.
